story.headline: US envoy meets Putin, Russia frees Hubbard
story.summary: Witkoff met Putin in St Petersburg a day after talks with Zelensky in Oslo.
story.display_body: US envoy Steve Witkoff met Vladimir Putin in St Petersburg on Wednesday 21 October, and Putin announced during the talks that Russia was releasing jailed American Stephen Hubbard. This was the ninth in-person meeting between the two, according to DW, and it came a day after Witkoff's talks with Volodymyr Zelensky in Oslo on Tuesday 20 October. The prime ministers of Norway and Finland and representatives of the EU and NATO also attended in Oslo; US Secretary of State Marco Rubio called those talks "positive" and said Witkoff would take "those ideas" to the Russian side. After Oslo, Zelensky said "very, very important" US intelligence sharing had been restored. Hubbard was captured in Ukraine and sentenced in 2024, at a closed trial, to seven years on mercenary charges he denies. DW reports that Putin also proposed discussing the restoration of US–Russian ties and a possible meeting with Donald Trump in Beijing. A separate dispute is still open: the Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday, citing US officials, that Elon Musk himself ordered the slowdown of SpaceX's satellite service for Ukraine; Rubio says the decision lies with the company, while Musk says only the US military and president can make it.
story.why: the talks follow Trump's open clash with Zelensky earlier this week, and Kyiv's access to US intelligence and satellite links now sits alongside the peace terms being discussed.

story.headline: Drone strike on Abyei market kills 153
story.summary: A drone strike on Amiet Market in disputed Abyei killed at least 153 people; South Sudan blames Sudan's army.
story.display_body: A drone strike on Amiet Market in the disputed Abyei region between Sudan and South Sudan on Monday 19 October killed at least 153 people, the region's caretaker information minister said on Tuesday 20 October. Yohanna Akol Ngor had given a toll of 73 the day before. He said some bodies had been burned to ashes and that around 8,000 people had been displaced. The drone hit a fuel depot, which caused a fire that was still burning on Tuesday. South Sudan's foreign ministry blamed Sudan's army and summoned Sudan's ambassador; neither it nor Abyei officials gave evidence. A senior Sudanese officer, speaking anonymously to AP, said the army targeted fuel tankers headed for the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and that the dead were RSF members and smugglers. UN spokesman Stéphane Dujarric said dozens of civilians, including women and children, were killed, without naming who carried out the strike. MSF (Doctors Without Borders) is treating more than 20 wounded, some with severe burns.
story.why: it is one of the deadliest single strikes of Sudan's war, which began in April 2023, and it drags a long-disputed border area, which diplomats say has become an RSF fuel route, further into the conflict.

story.headline: UN sees up to 2.8C of warming
story.summary: UNEP's Emissions Gap Report 2026 says 1.5C overshoot is now unavoidable and current policies lead to 2.8C.
story.display_body: The UN Environment Programme said on Wednesday 21 October that current policies put the world on course for up to 2.8°C of warming this century, and that overshooting the 1.5°C limit can no longer be avoided. Even if every national climate plan (NDC, a country's pledge under the Paris Agreement) is fully delivered, warming would reach 2.6°C. UNEP says both figures are worse than last year's because of the US withdrawal from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of past emissions, and that new pledges since then have made a "negligible" difference. The report's best case is a "lowest possible overshoot": peak warming of 1.7–1.8°C around mid-century, then a return to 1.5°C by 2100, with about a 50% chance. That would need emissions cuts of 18% by 2030, 45% by 2035 and 69% by 2040 compared with 2025 levels, against the 5–8% by 2030 that today's pledges would deliver. It would also need about 320 billion tonnes of CO2 to be removed from the air over the century, which UNEP calls uncertain.
story.why: the UN's own yardstick now says the 1.5°C goal can only be met by overshooting it and coming back, which sets the terms for this year's climate summit.

story.headline: Nigeria confirms first Ebola case
story.summary: WHO says Nigeria confirmed its first Ebola Bundibugyo case, a traveller from Uganda in Abuja.
story.display_body: Nigeria has confirmed its first case of Ebola Bundibugyo virus disease, in a woman in Abuja who had recently travelled from Uganda, the World Health Organization said on Wednesday 21 October. She developed symptoms on 7 October, four days after arriving, went to a private clinic in Abuja on 11 October, and was confirmed by laboratory test on 20 October. She is in isolation, and 44 contacts are being monitored. Nigeria is the fifth country to detect this strain since the Democratic Republic of the Congo declared an outbreak in mid-May; Congo has recorded more than 9,500 cases and 4,200 deaths as of 18 October, its deadliest outbreak ever. There is no approved vaccine for the Bundibugyo strain.
story.why: the nine days between the clinic visit and the diagnosis is the risk, in Africa's most populous country, because it leaves time for unnoticed spread.

story.headline: French 10-year yield tops 5%
story.summary: France's 10-year borrowing rate passed 5% for the first time since 2002.
story.display_body: France's ten-year borrowing cost rose above 5% on Wednesday 21 October for the first time since 2002, Le Monde reports. The gap with Germany's benchmark rate was 1.57 percentage points, after closing at 1.53 on Tuesday, its widest since November 2011. France now pays more to borrow than Italy (4.57%) or Spain (4.06%). Le Monde links the move to investor doubts, sharpened by the violence of 17–18 October, about whether the government can deliver a 2027 budget that plans €43 billion of new savings to bring the deficit to 5% of GDP.
story.why: a higher benchmark rate raises France's debt bill and, over time, its mortgage and business-loan rates.

story.headline: Iran claims three tankers hit mines
story.summary: Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed three more tankers struck mines south of the Strait of Hormuz.
story.display_body: Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed on Tuesday 20 October that three more oil tankers had hit Guard-laid mines south of the Strait of Hormuz. In statements carried by its Sepah News site and state TV, the Guards said two "violating" ships caught fire and were immobilised on a route they call "illegal", and that a third, carrying "two million barrels" of crude with its radar switched off, exploded. No independent confirmation from shipping authorities or the owners had been found by this edition.

story.headline: Double surnames return in 2027
story.summary: The Federal Council set 1 January 2027 for married couples to take an official double surname again.
story.display_body: From Friday 1 January 2027, married couples in Switzerland can again take an official double surname, the Federal Council decided on Wednesday 21 October. Double surnames have been barred since 2013; couples could only use an unofficial hyphenated "alliance name". The new double name can be written with or without a hyphen, but it stays unavailable for children. People who are already married can declare one at their civil-registry office from January. The alliance name can still appear on passports and ID cards during a transition period whose length has not been set yet. The changes to the civil-registry ordinance are due in November.

story.headline: Short-time work crisis rules to unwind
story.summary: The Federal Council plans a staggered return to normal short-time work compensation rules.
story.display_body: The Federal Council said on Wednesday 21 October that it plans to phase out, step by step, the crisis rules for short-time work compensation (RHT/Kurzarbeit, where unemployment insurance covers wages for hours lost). Today firms can claim for up to 24 months instead of the normal 12, and pay only one waiting day instead of three. The 24-month maximum runs until 31 January 2027. In December the government will decide whether to extend it from February and how to return to 12 months during 2027. The three-day waiting period is due back from 2028, with a consultation in spring 2027. The government points to its 17 September forecast of 1.7% growth in 2026 and 1.6% in 2027.
story.why: firms still relying on short-time work lose the extended cushion gradually through 2027 rather than all at once, and the government can still pause if the outlook worsens.

story.headline: Wyssmann enters SVP Federal Council race
story.summary: Solothurn SVP national councillor Remy Wyssmann is running to succeed Guy Parmelin.
story.display_body: Solothurn SVP national councillor Rémy Wyssmann said on Wednesday 21 October that he is running to succeed Federal Councillor Guy Parmelin. The 59-year-old lawyer and notary has sat in the National Council since December 2023. He is only the second declared candidate after Geneva national councillor Céline Amaudruz, after several better-known names ruled themselves out. He said he would stand up for the middle class. The SVP parliamentary group picks its ticket on Friday 20 November, and the Federal Assembly elects on Wednesday 9 December.

story.headline: Court bars PostFinance voiceprints
story.summary: The Federal Administrative Court ruled PostFinance needs explicit consent to store callers' voiceprints.
story.display_body: The Federal Administrative Court has ruled that PostFinance may not create voiceprints of hotline callers without their explicit consent, SRF reported on Wednesday 21 October. Since autumn 2018, PostFinance's hotline recorded a voice profile of callers to recognise them next time, unless they told the agent they objected. The court agreed with the Federal Data Protection Commissioner that this opt-out is not enough: a voice reveals emotions, health and personal traits, so an opt-in is required. PostFinance must get consent for existing profiles or delete them. The ruling can be appealed to the Federal Supreme Court.
story.why: it sets a test for any Swiss company using voice biometrics for customer identification.

story.headline: Bern backs cement carbon border levy
story.summary: The Federal Council backed a bill for a carbon border charge on imported cement, with a trigger mechanism.
story.display_body: The Federal Council on Wednesday 21 October backed a National Council committee's bill for a carbon levy at the border on imported cement, but asked for a trigger mechanism because of the risks to trade. The bill responds to parliamentary initiative 21.432. It would make importers declare cement-based goods and pay a CO2 charge, matching what Swiss cement plants pay under the emissions-trading system and copying, for this one sector, the EU's carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM). Cement is the largest emitter among the Swiss plants in emissions trading.

story.headline: Google grows high-fidelity magic states
story.summary: Google grows high-fidelity magic states on a quantum chip.
story.display_body: Error-corrected quantum computers can do the "easy" class of operations (Clifford gates) cheaply on encoded qubits, but those alone cannot outperform a classical computer. Universal computing also needs at least one non-Clifford gate, such as the T gate. The usual route is to prepare special "magic states" and consume them, and making them clean enough has meant magic state distillation: a factory that burns many noisy copies to produce one good one, often the most expensive part of a fault-tolerant design. Magic state cultivation, proposed by Google researchers in 2024, instead grows a single magic state inside a small error-correcting code, repeatedly checks it and throws it away at the first sign of an error, then transfers ("code-switches") it into a standard surface code. This paper is the first experimental test of the whole procedure on a superconducting processor. Cultivation cut the error by a factor of 40, reaching a magic-state fidelity of at least 0.9999(1), bounded with a fault-tolerant measurement protocol the team developed for the purpose. The cost is visible in the numbers: only 8% of attempts were kept. A separate theory preprint from early October argues that realistic, non-destructive checking can make cultivation's logical error rates orders of magnitude worse at the costs previously reported, so the overhead question is not closed.
story.why: This moves the cheapest known recipe for the hardest ingredient of a useful quantum computer from simulation to hardware. A 92% discard rate is affordable only if attempts are fast and cheap, which is the next thing to establish.

story.headline: COHERENT pins neutrino-nucleus scattering on germanium
story.summary: COHERENT makes its most precise measurement of neutrinos bouncing off whole nuclei.
story.display_body: Neutrinos interact so weakly that detectors usually need tonnes of material. At low energies, though, a neutrino can scatter off an entire nucleus at once, with all its protons and neutrons responding together. This "coherent elastic neutrino-nucleus scattering" (CEvNS) is much more likely than other interactions but leaves only a tiny nuclear recoil to detect. COHERENT first observed it in 2017. Here the collaboration used Ge-Mini, a germanium detector array at Oak Ridge's Spallation Neutron Source, a pulsed neutrino source whose energy and timing are well understood. From 4.69×10²² protons on target they counted 124 (+14/−12) events and measured a cross-section 0.98 ± 0.10 (statistical) ± 0.10 (systematic) times the Standard Model value. They describe it as the most precise CEvNS measurement to date. The source's timing also let them separate muon-neutrino and electron-neutrino scattering rates, tightening limits on "non-standard" neutrino interactions carried by heavy new particles.
story.why: The Standard Model passes again, now at roughly 15% precision. The same recoils form the "neutrino fog" that next-generation dark-matter detectors will hit, so pinning down the rate on germanium helps those experiments too.

story.headline: Levitated nanoparticle detects single gas collisions
story.summary: A levitated nanoparticle feels the kick of single gas molecules.
story.display_body: A glass nanoparticle held in a laser beam in vacuum ("optically levitated") is isolated from almost everything, which makes it an extremely sensitive force sensor. The Yale group let individual krypton, xenon and sulphur hexafluoride molecules hit such a particle and resolved each collision as a separate momentum kick, with reconstructed impulses as small as 200 keV/c. That is roughly the momentum a single heavy molecule at room temperature carries. The measured rates matched theory and gave the partial pressure of each gas directly. The shape of the kick spectrum also revealed properties of the particle's surface, including its temperature.
story.why: Counting collisions one by one is a new way to measure pressure from first principles, without calibrating against another gauge. The same sensitivity is what levitated-sensor proposals need to detect recoils from dark-matter particles or neutrinos.

story.headline: Fast warming could tip East Antarctic basins
story.summary: Fast warming could tip two East Antarctic basins before their thresholds.
story.display_body: Where Antarctic ice rests on bedrock below sea level and the bed slopes downward inland, retreat can become self-sustaining: the further the grounding line (where ice lifts off the bed and floats) retreats, the thicker the ice at the edge and the faster it flows out. This "marine ice-sheet instability" is usually studied as a threshold, a warming level past which retreat runs away. As ice thins, the bedrock slowly rises back up ("glacial isostatic adjustment"), which pushes against retreat. The Madrid–AWI team coupled an ice-sheet model to a bedrock model and sampled the uncertain viscosity of the mantle underneath. If warming is fast compared with that rebound, the stabilising uplift arrives too late, and retreat can start below the equilibrium threshold. This is "rate-induced tipping". West Antarctica is unlikely to tip this way because its mantle is runny enough to rebound quickly. The Recovery and Aurora subglacial basins in East Antarctica are likely to tip this way even at warming rates lower than today's. Depending on mantle viscosity, the effect lowers the critical global warming level by up to 0.5 K.
story.why: East Antarctica is usually seen as the stable part of the continent. This is a model result, but it says the speed of warming matters as well as its peak, and it singles out two basins that hold a large amount of ice.

story.headline: Holocene records shrink Arctic winter ice projections
story.summary: Ancient sea-ice records point to less Arctic winter ice than models project.
story.display_body: Climate models disagree most about Arctic sea ice in winter, the season when ice cover controls how much heat escapes from ocean to atmosphere. The team compiled an Arctic-wide database of sediment biomarkers (molecules left by algae that live in or near sea ice) from the mid-Holocene, 5,000–7,000 years ago, a period warmer than pre-industrial. They used a statistical "proxy system model" to compare these records quantitatively with each climate model's simulation of the same period, then weighted the models by how well they matched. The weighting accounts for models that share code and for the season the biomarkers actually record. It removes the ensemble's bias and cuts its uncertainty by 85%, down to the level of normal year-to-year variability. Applied to the future, the weighted projections put winter sea-ice extent nearly 1 million km² below previous estimates across the coming decades and emissions scenarios.
story.why: Less winter ice means more ocean heat reaching the Arctic atmosphere, which feeds into Arctic ecosystems and mid-latitude weather, Europe's included. The result depends on how far the mid-Holocene, driven by orbital changes rather than CO₂, is a fair test for the future.

story.headline: Catalyst lasts longest at the freezing point
story.summary: A water-splitting catalyst lasts longest right at the freezing point.
story.display_body: Splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen needs a catalyst for the oxygen side. Cheap manganese dioxide works but corrodes, dissolving as permanganate. Usually lowering the temperature just slows everything down. Here it slowed the corrosion more than the useful reaction, so lifetime improved more than activity fell. Below 0 °C, in supercooled electrolyte, degradation sped up again, the opposite of normal (Arrhenius) temperature behaviour. The best balance sits near 0 °C.
story.why: Temperature is a cheap control knob that is usually ignored. The authors point to electrolysers in winter or polar conditions. This is a lab result on a single catalyst.

story.headline: One-gram wireless microscope images mouse cortex
story.summary: A one-gram wireless microscope records 8,500 neurons in free-roaming mice.
story.display_body: Imaging large parts of the brain at single-neuron resolution normally means a heavy benchtop microscope and a head-fixed animal. Head-mounted miniscopes free the animal but are tethered by cables and see a small patch. Airscope is a 1.0-gram wireless "mesoscope" (a wide-field microscope) with 4 µm resolution across a 6 mm field of view at 12.5 frames per second. An aspheric lens design makes it 2.84 times shorter than previous miniature microscopes, and a custom wireless link streams calcium imaging, in which neurons light up when active, from more than 8,500 neurons per mouse. The authors say that is a 25-fold increase. They imaged mice in room-sized arenas, while swimming, and several animals at once. Activity across the dorsal cortex predicted which of two competing mice would win, and simultaneous brain and spinal-cord recordings showed the spinal cord influencing the cortex during fear conditioning.
story.why: Much of what is known about cortical activity comes from restrained animals doing simple tasks. A device light enough for natural social behaviour opens those questions to large-scale recording. The behavioural findings are demonstrations of the tool, not settled neuroscience.

story.headline: Psilocybin's rewiring and trip use different neurons
story.summary: Psilocybin's synapse remodelling and its "trip" use different neurons.
story.display_body: Psilocybin acts mainly on serotonin 2A receptors (5-HT2A) and is being tested for depression. A central question is whether its lasting benefit needs the hallucinogenic experience, or whether its effect on synapses (neuroplasticity) can be separated out. In mice, the team found that psilocybin both builds and matures new synapses and speeds the removal of existing ones. Switching 5-HT2A on or off only in cortical layer-5 pyramidal neurons showed that signalling in those cells is necessary and sufficient for the rewiring. It was not needed for the head-twitch response, the standard mouse stand-in for a hallucination.
story.why: This supports the idea that non-hallucinogenic psychedelic-like drugs could keep the plasticity without the trip. The head-twitch response is only a proxy for human hallucinations, and the study measures synapses, not mood.

story.headline: Infused antibody-toxin clears phase 1 in glioblastoma
story.summary: An antibody-toxin infused into recurrent brain tumours passes a phase 1 test.
story.display_body: Glioblastoma almost always recurs, and few drugs reach the tumour through the blood–brain barrier. D2C7-ATC is an antibody that recognises both normal EGFR and its tumour-specific mutant EGFRvIII, fused to a bacterial toxin. Rather than injecting it into the blood, the Duke team infused it directly into the tumour through catheters, using slow pressure-driven "convection-enhanced delivery". The single-site trial treated 81 patients with recurrent malignant glioma with a single infusion. Most treatment-related side effects were mild to moderate (grades 1–2), and four patients had dose-limiting toxicities at the highest dose. Among 72 patients with IDH-wild-type recurrent glioblastoma, the most common and aggressive form, median overall survival was 7.9 months. In exploratory subgroups (low tumour antibody reactivity, or low IL-8 in blood after treatment), median survival was about 17 months. Biomarkers point to an immune response inside and outside the tumour.
story.why: The trial sets a recommended dose and shows the delivery method is tolerable. With one arm and no controls, the authors' claim that it prolongs survival in a subset rests on post-hoc biomarker splits that a randomised trial would need to confirm.

story.headline: No sub-solar black holes in O4b gravitational data
story.summary: LIGO, Virgo and KAGRA find no sub-solar-mass black holes, tightening dark-matter limits.
story.display_body: Stars cannot collapse into black holes lighter than the Sun, so a merger involving one would point to new physics. One candidate is primordial black holes, formed in the early universe and proposed as part of dark matter. Another is "dark black holes" made by dark matter that can cool and collapse. The detectors searched data from April 2024 to January 2025 (O4b, the first stretch of the current run in which Virgo joined both LIGO sites) for binaries with a lighter component of 0.2–1 solar masses. Two of three independent search pipelines flagged outlier candidates, but none was significant enough to count as evidence. The resulting merger-rate limits range from 50 to 5,000 per cubic gigaparsec per year, depending on the masses. For primordial black holes that formed binaries early, at most 1.8–3.2% of dark matter can be in 1-solar-mass objects, and at most 10–18% at 0.35 solar masses. The collaboration's own science summary describes O4b as the most sensitive network it has run so far.
story.why: The collaboration calls these the most stringent limits to date on sub-solar-mass mergers. Each null result narrows the range of masses where primordial black holes could still make up a large share of dark matter. Virgo is a European detector, run from Italy.

story.headline: First hot Jupiter found in orbital resonance
story.summary: TESS finds the first hot Jupiter locked in an orbital resonance.
story.display_body: Hot Jupiters, gas giants orbiting their stars in days, usually have no close neighbours. That has been read as a sign that they arrived through violent scattering that cleared out other planets. TOI-3686 c is a hot Jupiter on a 5.08-day orbit whose transits arrive up to 40 minutes early or late, one of the largest such timing swings seen for a hot Jupiter. Those swings led the team to a second planet in the NASA TESS data, a sub-Neptune on a 2.54-day orbit whose transits swing by 10 hours, about 16% of its period. Modelling the transits together with radial-velocity measurements shows the pair sits deep in a 2:1 resonance: the inner planet completes exactly two orbits for each of the outer's. It is the only hot Jupiter currently known in a truly resonant configuration, and the system is younger than about 1 billion years.
story.why: A resonance this tidy is hard to get from scattering. It points instead to a quiet migration through the gas disk, the same path thought to build compact chains of small planets. At least some hot Jupiters may have formed the gentle way.

story.headline: Ionising light escapes young starbursts early
story.summary: Ionising light escapes young starbursts early, before supernova winds shut the door.
story.display_body: About a billion years after the Big Bang, ultraviolet light ionised the hydrogen between galaxies ("reionisation"). Small, compact star-forming galaxies are the main suspects, but how much of their ionising "Lyman continuum" light gets out, and what controls it, is uncertain. The team took medium-resolution spectra of six similar nearby compact starbursts of different ages and followed both the launch of a galactic wind and the fraction of Lyman continuum that escapes. Escape peaks early, within about 3 million years, while radiation and stellar winds dominate and before a fast galactic wind has developed. In older systems they see faster, dustier winds and less escape. Their reading is that supernova-driven winds loaded with gas and dust suppress escape within the first ~10 million years.
story.why: JWST is finding many such compact galaxies in the early universe. Knowing that the ionising light escapes in a brief early window changes how their contribution to reionisation should be counted. Six galaxies is a small sample.

story.headline: Bulge cluster VVV CL001 dated to 13.4 billion years
story.summary: A bulge globular cluster dates to 13.4 billion years.
story.display_body: VVV CL001 is a very metal-poor globular cluster behind heavy dust in the Galactic bulge, so its distance and age have been poorly known. Combining deep ground-based infrared imaging with Hubble photometry, the team derives a distance of 7.34 ± 0.46 kpc and an age of 13.4 ± 0.4 billion years. That makes it a strong candidate for the oldest globular cluster in the Milky Way.
story.why: The oldest clusters set a lower limit on the age of the Galaxy and the universe (13.8 billion years). The age's uncertainty overlaps with other very old clusters, so "oldest" is a candidacy, not a ranking.

story.headline: Large Magellanic Cloud still ringing from collision
story.summary: The Large Magellanic Cloud is still ringing from a collision with its neighbour.
story.display_body: Distance maps built from "red clump" stars, a type of star with a known brightness, show that the outer disk of the Large Magellanic Cloud sits about 1.2 kpc out of the plane of its centre and bends into an S-shaped warp reaching 3.6 kpc. A simulation of a direct collision with the Small Magellanic Cloud sets the outer disk oscillating vertically with a ~600-million-year period and matches the observed offset about 260 million years after impact. It underpredicts the warp's size by a factor of 4–5.
story.why: This adds to evidence that the two Clouds collided recently, and shows that encounters between dwarf galaxies can reshape whole disks. The warp mismatch shows the model is still incomplete.
